analysis.one_liner: Bans new mining on about 1.1 million acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committee without a vote after a single hearing; no floor action ever happened.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Raúl Grijalva's bill would have permanently removed roughly 1,068,908 acres of federal land — the Tusayan Ranger District, land near Kanab Creek, and House Rock Valley — from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing. The goal was to keep uranium and other mining out of the watersheds that drain into the Grand Canyon and its Colorado River tributaries. People or companies who already held valid mining rights would have kept them. The bill never left committee; it got one hearing and no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People who rely on water draining into the Grand Canyon and the Colorado River, since mining around the canyon risks contaminating groundwater and streams. It also protects the national park's surroundings and the public's recreation land from new mine development.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grand Canyon-area water users and park visitors

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws roughly 1,068,908 acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, keeping new mines out of the watersheds feeding the canyon [S2][S3].
The withdrawal is permanent (subject only to valid existing rights), unlike administrative protections that a future administration can reverse [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies and prospectors who wanted to stake new uranium and mineral claims on the affected land, and would lose access to roughly a million acres. Existing valid claims would have been honored.

drawbacks.text: Existing mining rights are grandfathered in, so any mines already authorized before the bill would continue and could still affect the watershed [S3].

The bill locks up federal minerals that could supply domestic uranium production, a cost critics of canyon-area withdrawals have raised, and it is written to block entry for all minerals, not just uranium [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection it offered was broad and permanent, aimed at a specific, widely recognized risk — mining in the waterways feeding the Grand Canyon — and it respected existing rights. The cost falls on a narrow set of mineral claimholders rather than on the public. The main design limitation is the grandfather clause, which leaves previously established operations untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, got one subcommittee hearing in June 2008, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on March 11, 2008, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day [S1][S5].
Three Democratic cosponsors joined the bill; no Republican cosponsored it [S4].
The bill was split between two subcommittees — National Parks, Forests and Public Lands, and Energy and Mineral Resources — on March 13, 2008 [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held June 5, 2008, but no committee markup or vote followed, and the bill never reached the House floor [S5].
The bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining interests keep open the option of staking new claims on about a million acres near the Grand Canyon, and no new legal barrier to mining in those watersheds was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining interests near the Grand Canyon

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.role: Sponsor; member, House Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw about 1,068,908 acres around the Grand Canyon from new mining and mineral leasing [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never brought it to a committee vote or the House floor during the rest of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all four supporters on record were House Democrats and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar new mining claims and mineral leasing on roughly 1.1 million acres around the Grand Canyon, closing off access to minerals these companies wanted to develop. Mining in canyon watersheds is the exact risk the bill targets, so the industry's interest runs directly against the water protection the public would get.

industries.industry: Mineral leasing and geothermal energy developers
industries.note: The bill also withdraws the land from mineral and geothermal leasing, shutting out developers of oil, gas, and geothermal resources on those acres.
